extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, media critics, and researchers interested in journalism ethics and news production
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the quality, sourcing and integrity of daily news journalism (particularly investigative and national newspaper reporting) as discussed in Nick Davies' Flat Earth News and its coverage. Emphasises practices such as fact-checking, original investigation, sources interrogation, and the structural influences on news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter-led fact-checking and investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Only 12% of the examined stories were provably based on material that the reporters had fact-checked and investigated themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page presents reporter-led fact-checking and original investigation as a central standard of routine, day-to-day journalism — but the research Davies cites shows this is often absent. A high-quality story should be provably based on reporters' own fact-checking and investigation rather than unverified secondary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: News judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: "Everyday practices of news judgement" are identified as, in theory, central to routine journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether journalists exercised appropriate news judgement in choosing, framing and prioritising stories. The page treats news judgement as an expected norm that is frequently not met in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance is listed among the everyday practices (alongside fact-checking, criticising and interrogating sources) that should be central to journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether reporting presents a balanced view, includes multiple perspectives, and avoids one-sided presentation. The book argues balance often fails in routine coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticising and interrogating sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticising and interrogating sources is named as a routine journalistic practice that should occur but is often the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality journalism should question sources, challenge claims, and not accept information at face value. The page highlights lack of interrogation of sources as a common failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracing origins of stories / provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers examined the origins of 2,000 stories carried by major UK papers to determine how stories originated and whether they were independently checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful evaluative criterion is whether a story’s provenance is transparent and whether its origins can be traced to original reporting rather than secondary or PR-originated copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'churnalism' (reliance on prepackaged material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Davies and cited Press Gazette pieces criticise 'churnalism' — the replacement of original reporting with recycled or uncritically republished material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice is to avoid churnalism: reporters should not simply reproduce press releases or wire copy without verification, attribution, and added reporting. The page positions churnalism as a negative pattern undermining truth-telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meticulous research and evidentiary weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews praise the book as 'meticulously researched' and note Davies 'amassed an overwhelming weight of evidence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative work (and by extension evaluations of journalism) should rest on thorough, careful research and substantial documentary or empirical evidence; reviewers treat this as a mark of credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of primary documents and documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Press Gazette series referenced concrete documentary materials (e.g., a fax, phone numbers, phone bills) in assessing stories such as the David Kelly case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality investigative reporting should make use of primary documents and verifiable evidence; inclusion and citation of such materials strengthens credibility and supports claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial willingness to publish investigative work
rubrics_metrics.description: Press Gazette serialised Flat Earth News 'when every national newspaper – including The Guardian – declined to do so', indicating editorial gatekeeping affects what investigative work reaches the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard for the ecosystem: editors and outlets should be willing to publish investigative pieces even if they are controversial or challenging to powerful interests; refusal to publish can indicate structural problems affecting news quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural and commercial influences on news quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Davies' thesis: the problem is structural — corporations operating under commercial logic have taken over newsrooms, resulting in fewer journalists and increased workloads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news quality, consider structural factors such as ownership, commercial pressures, staffing levels and workloads, which can impede fact-checking, original reporting and editorial scrutiny. These systemic conditions are proposed as root causes of declines in standards.
